newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-AWB says wheat price over-corrected.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-AWB says wheat price over-corrected.

text.p: The Australian Wheat Board (AWB), a major player in the world wheat market, believes wheat prices have reached an over-correction zone, does not believe the United States will introduce wheat export subsidies, and thinks intense world wheat competition will stop short of a trade war.

Ron Storey, the top merchandising executive of the AWB, which will export about 15 million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97, told Reuters the world wheat price appeared to be at or near the bottom of its downward curve.

"I think we saw the market over-correct on the upside as a result of fear and panic about shortages in April/May," he said in an interview. "Our feeling is that we're probably in the process (now) of over-correcting on the downside," he said.
After a A$100 a tonne price fall over the past four or five months, the market was still trying to find the bottom, he said. But a slide of the recent magnitude would not continue unabated.
"We're probably in the over-correction phase," he said. "If we're not at the bottom we're at the bottom of that curve."

In Australian pool price terms, wheat prices have fallen 30 percent since May to A$175.00 a tonne. The latest pool price cut, a severe A$15.00 a tonne earlier this week, sparked dismay in the Australian industry and prompted public fears that the world was headed toward another wheat war.
Storey does not foresee the outbreak of a world wheat war of the seriousness of the 1980s, when stocks swamped markets and export subsidies were used to buy market share.
"It's a war every day as far as the market is concerned," he said. "Certainly competition is intense, given supplies from Artgentina, ourselves, Canada and Europe."
But recent EU subsidies were on relatively limited volume, there was still no across-the-board world onslaught of subsidies, and no subsidies from the United States, he said.
Speculation has circulated for months that the United States would introduce Export Enhancement Program (EEP) subsidies and still it had not, Storey said.
"I don't think that they're inclined to. There are certainly calls for it from within the U.S., but that's not unusual."
The reality was that low supplies had left the U.S. export programme going very well, he said.
"They don't need subsidies to sell everything they've got this year. So it really would not seem to make too much sense to have subsidies to sell a crop you haven't got," Storey said.
Storey saw a theoretical possibility of very quick downturn turning upward with equal speed.
But increased export demand would be required to turn the market around in a significant way, he added.
The near-term prospect of this was not good, with most importing countries seemingly fairly comfortable, he said.
